findings.finding: Raising the shutdown budget to at least the 45 s request deadline is a change to a number the private deployment repository owns; done alone it makes shutdown worse than today, because the kubelet SIGKILLs at terminationGracePeriodSeconds whatever the process believes.
findings.answer: Decision D3: the budget is derived, not chosen - writeTimeout = requestDeadline + 15 s becomes a named constant and shutdownTimeout equals it (60 s), and the process logs `broker stop budget drain=<d> shutdown=60s total=<d+60s>` at boot. INFRA-62's prescribed guard (a test in the owning module reading the dependent's rendered golden) cannot cross repositories, so the boot log and operate.md's arithmetic replace it, and section 6 of the plan hands INFRA-240 the inequality its grace period must satisfy.

findings.finding: 'Long enough for Kubernetes to stop sending it traffic' has no meaning in this repository: the readiness probe's period and failure threshold live in INFRA-240's repository.
findings.answer: Decision D1: the drain is sized to outlast EndpointSlice propagation, not a probe, because removal from the EndpointSlice starts at the deletion timestamp concurrently with termination (docs/solutions/infra/...INFRA-62.md lines 27-33) - the same thing Dispatch's own 5 s preStop wait is sized for. Default 5 s. Failing the health check stays, because a probe-driven removal and any readiness-reading ingress also stop sending, but it is not what sets the length. Recorded as this plan's one departure from the spec's stated mechanism.

findings.finding: /healthz is the documented liveness probe as well as the readiness probe, so failing it during the drain can have the kubelet kill the container mid-drain.
findings.answer: Decision D4: one route, flipped to 503 SHUTTING_DOWN, no /readyz. No pod in this repository sets a liveness probe at all (infra/gcp/dispatch_kube.go sets ReadinessProbe and StartupProbe only), operate.md's 'Use it for liveness and readiness' sentence is rewritten to readiness-only and becomes a contract line for INFRA-240, and the worst case if that is ignored is an earlier kill during a termination already under way - today's behaviour, never worse. A /readyz row would cost a route row, a refgen comment, a named response type and AGENTS.md's hand-counted route total.

findings.finding: 'It must not need a new piece of infrastructure' is unverified for LISTEN/NOTIFY: a transaction pooler (pgbouncer in transaction mode, RDS Proxy) in front of Postgres would not carry a long-lived LISTEN, and the broker's database path is not visible in this repository.
findings.answer: Plan section 6.4 and section 8: the architect must confirm with the deployment that BROKER_DATABASE_URL is a session path with room for one more connection per pod, before the implementer's phase completes. The design degrades safely either way - a listener that cannot hold a connection logs every redial and the five-minute reload remains the backstop - and the two-process tests prove the mechanism on real Postgres.

findings.finding: policy.Current.RefreshOne has two callers and the issue speaks only about the HTTP route; putting the notify inside RefreshOne would fan out every miss-path reread too.
findings.answer: Decision D5: only POST /v1/secrets/{name}/reread notifies. The miss path (internal/broker/requests/machine_state.go:358-361) stays local, which is what 'a new secret heals itself on first use' already promises, and fanning it out would spend every peer a DescribeSecret (two GCP metadata reads) for a name that peer may never be asked for.

findings.finding: Notifying only on a real change needs a 'changed' result RefreshOne does not have today.
findings.answer: Decision D6: the route notifies on every 200 and on no refusal, so no signature changes. Notify-on-change was rejected for a hole as well as its churn: a pod whose own five-minute reload already caught the retag answers 'unchanged' and tells nobody, leaving the peer stale. Notify-always is also the arithmetic the spec's own halving assumes.

findings.finding: Loop, self-delivery and burst duplication in a LISTEN/NOTIFY fan-out are unaddressed: Postgres delivers to the sending process's own listening session too, and a notification-driven refresh that notified again would ping-pong.
findings.answer: Decision D7: the payload is {"name","sender"} with the sender's boot uuid, a listener drops its own, and a notification-driven reread never notifies - the fan-out is one hop by construction. Burst cost is bounded by the sender side alone, which is what decision D8's halving sizes; the receiving side spends no token, as the spec requires.

findings.finding: 'The broker-wide limit itself is halved' does not say rate, burst, which of the three reread limits, or what happens at a replica count other than two.
findings.answer: Decision D8: both broker-wide buckets halve in both dimensions - DefaultRereadOverallLimit {250ms,10} becomes {500ms,5} and GCPRereadOverallLimit {1s,10} becomes {2s,5}, whose quota arithmetic is restated for the fleet (the same 120 metadata reads a minute). Retry-After follows Every, so the default stays 1 s and the GCP bucket's becomes 2 s, and both figures are carried into operate.md and the troubleshooting guide. The per-address, launcher and token-endpoint limits are unchanged and their comments gain the per-process sentence the spec's fourth bullet asks for. Each halved comment states the invariant (replicas times this rate is the fleet's cap) rather than the replica count alone.

findings.finding: storetest.URL gives each test a schema on one shared database while LISTEN/NOTIFY and the migration advisory lock are database-wide, so concurrent tests would hear each other.
findings.answer: Decision D9 and work item W8: the channel is one package constant (pglisten requires that), and the two-process rows and the reread package's own tests take a fresh database from a new storetest.DatabaseURL helper rather than a schema. Production is one database per deployment, so no per-deployment channel name is needed.

findings.finding: The 'two processes migrating at once' row has no harness - every existing way to get a broker database hands back an already-migrated schema - and no stated expected outcome.
findings.answer: W8 gives storetest.DatabaseURL an unmigrated database, and test T4 states the assertions: both processes log 'broker listening' and answer /healthz 200, broker_schema_migrations holds each version exactly once, and the loser's wait on pg_advisory_xact_lock is unbounded by design, which the test says in prose.

findings.finding: Nothing says which connection the listener holds; a LISTEN on a pooled connection ends when the pool recycles it, and a rig that opened one would reach the daemon's contract tests.
findings.answer: Decision D10 and work item W3: store gains Listener(ctx) built as Dispatch's is - a one-connection pool from the shared pool's configuration, so BeforeConnect keeps minting RDS IAM tokens on every redial, acquired and hijacked. It is wired in cmd/broker only; brokertest.NewRig and packages/daemon's internal/agentsecrets contract test open none. The cost, one extra Postgres connection per pod, is handed to INFRA-240.

findings.finding: What happens to the 'within seconds' promise while the listener is redialing is unstated; a full catch-up refresh on every reconnect would cost each pod a whole-namespace read.
findings.answer: Decision D11: OnConnected only logs, and the documented promise becomes 'within seconds, except while a pod's listener is redialing, where the next five-minute reload is the backstop' - which is today's behaviour, not a regression. Test T3 makes the promise machine-checkable: the peer refuses the narrowed secret within 10 s of the reread's 200, two orders of magnitude inside the five-minute reload.

findings.finding: The spec's claim that everything else is already safe for several pods holds for the authority paths, but several pieces of process-local state are not shared: every rate limiter, the per-enrollment miss-reread budget, the GCP read cache and the 30-second minted-secret recheck.
findings.answer: Decision D13b: this plan documents them (the per-process comments the spec's fourth bullet asks for) and changes none, since each is a flood guard whose doubling is a load question rather than an authority question. Both this and the device-code 500 go to the architect as findings in the completion report.

findings.finding: The two acceptance tests name no expected outcomes, no CI lane, and no way to hold a request past ten seconds.
findings.answer: Plan section 4: eight rows, each with its surface, its command and its assertion; a new broker-multiprocess CI job modelled on dispatch-multiprocess, gated on the same envoy change filter; and the in-flight mechanism named rather than left to the implementer - the test holds the machine login's oauth_refresh_tokens row with `select ... for update` so a refresh grant blocks inside RotateRefreshToken's own `for update`, with no sleep in the broker.

findings.finding: Two scope questions: whether the device-code loser's 500 server_error is this issue's to fix, and that acceptance line 3 (merged, released, digest) cannot be satisfied inside an implementing phase.
findings.answer: Decision D13a: the test pins the invariant (exactly one exchange succeeds, exactly one credential is minted) and records the loser's observed status without pinning it; the 500 goes to the architect as a finding rather than a silent fix, since the deliverables name no OAuth change. Plan section 7: the implementer's scope ends at a merge-ready head, and the merge commit and released digest are read with the commands named there and reported in the implementer's production check after the close.

specDepartures.spec: The spec says Kubernetes removes a pod from its Service when its health check fails, so a drain that fails the check is what stops traffic reaching a stopping pod, and the drain must last 'long enough for Kubernetes to stop sending it traffic'.
specDepartures.plan: The drain is sized to outlast the EndpointSlice propagation that a pod's deletion starts, defaulting to 5 seconds and configurable as BROKER_DRAIN_SECONDS, rather than to a readiness probe's periodSeconds times failureThreshold (about 35 seconds at this repository's own probe numbers). The program still fails /healthz for the whole drain, as the spec asks.
specDepartures.evidence: docs/solutions/infra/a-pre-stop-wait-is-paid-out-of-the-pods-grace-and-the-constant-that-sizes-it-lives-in-another-module-INFRA-62.md lines 27-33: 'A pod's removal from its EndpointSlice starts when the deletion timestamp appears, concurrently with the kubelet beginning termination... The pre-stop hook is what runs alongside propagation and outlasts it.' packages/envoy/infra/gcp/dispatch_kube.go sizes Dispatch's own 5 s preStop wait on exactly that, and its readiness probe is periodSeconds 10 with failureThreshold 3.
